title: Fourth sense: natural as having its cause in nature; the body's temperament and the tree of life
source_text: XVII. Rursum addit naturale dici id quod in ipsa natura causam habet. Et etiam, inquit, hoc pacto immortalitas fuit primo homini quodammodo naturalis. Nam in optima humani corporis temperie tanquam interna causa, & in ligno vitae tanquam externa causa (quarum utraque ad illum effectum naturalis erat) immortalitas consistebat.
pass_a_gloss: Again he adds that that is called natural which has its cause in nature itself. And also, he says, in this manner immortality was to the first man in a certain way natural. For immortality consisted in the best temperament of the human body as an internal cause, and in the tree of life as an external cause (each of which was natural toward that effect).
pass_b_english: He adds that what has its cause in nature itself is called natural. "In this way too," he says, "immortality was in a manner natural to the first man. For it rested on the excellent balance of the human body as its inner cause and on the tree of life as its outer cause, and each of these was a natural cause of that effect."

lemmas.gloss: the excellent balance (temperament) of the human body

choices.why: Estius hedges with quodammodo; the English keeps the hedge.
